### Birth, Boyhood, and the Taming of Bucephalus ()
Cite as: [Source: "Birth, Boyhood, and the Taming of Bucephalus"]
Principle: Plutarch announces he is writing a life, not a history, and proves it immediately: a boy's questions to Persian envoys and his handling of one unmanageable horse tell us more about Alexander than any battle count could.
- Plutarch states his purpose up front: he is writing lives, not histories, and will favor a revealing "expression or a jest" over an exhaustive account of great armaments and battles, the same way a portrait painter lingers on the face rather than the whole body.
- Alexander's birth is wrapped in omens: Olympias dreamed of a thunderbolt striking her body before conception, Philip dreamed of sealing her womb with the image of a lion, and diviners read both as signs of a lion-hearted son; a serpent later found sleeping beside Olympias reportedly cooled Philip's affection for her, amid rumors she practiced the ecstatic serpent-rites of Orphic and Bacchic worship.
- Alexander was born the same day the temple of Diana at Ephesus burned down, and Philip received news of his son's birth in the same hour as word of a victory over the Illyrians and of his own horse winning at the Olympic games, three simultaneous successes diviners took to mean the child would be invincible.
- As a boy, Alexander showed little interest in athletic contests for their own sake, saying he would only race if he could compete against kings, and he favored music, poetry, and hunting over boxing or the pancratium.
- Left to entertain visiting Persian ambassadors in his father's absence, the young Alexander impressed them not with childish talk but with pointed, substantive questions about travel distances, the character of the Persian king, and the size of his forces.
- Alexander tamed the horse Bucephalas, which no one else could mount, by noticing it feared its own shadow and turning it to face the sun before calmly mounting it; Philip, watching him ride back in triumph, wept and told him "Macedonia is too little for thee," urging him to seek a kingdom worthy of himself.
- Philip brought in Aristotle to tutor Alexander, rewarding him by rebuilding and repopulating Aristotle's demolished home city of Stagira; Alexander later wrote to Aristotle protesting the publication of his esoteric doctrines, saying he would rather excel others in knowledge than in power.
- Alexander's love of learning carried into adulthood: he kept Aristotle's annotated copy of Homer's Iliad under his pillow with his dagger, calling it a portable treasure of military knowledge, and he practiced enough medicine, learned partly from Aristotle, to prescribe remedies for sick friends.

### Accession: Thebes Destroyed, Athens Spared ()
Cite as: [Source: "Accession: Thebes Destroyed, Athens Spared"]
Principle: At twenty, inheriting a kingdom ringed by enemies, Alexander answers every counsel of caution with speed, and the resulting contrast, a leveled Thebes against a spared Athens, becomes the template for how he will use terror and mercy as matched tools for the rest of his life.
- Alexander became king at twenty over a kingdom "beset on all sides" by hostile neighboring tribes and unsettled Greek city-states still resentful of Philip's incomplete conquest; advisers urged him to court the restless Greeks with patience and concession.
- He rejected that advice as weak, judging that any appearance of yielding would only invite more rebellion, and instead launched a rapid campaign north to the Danube, where he decisively defeated Syrmus and the Triballians.
- Hearing that Thebes had revolted with Athenian encouragement, he marched south through Thermopylae so fast that he made good on his boast to Demosthenes, who had mocked him as a "child" and a "youth," that he would appear a grown man at the walls of Athens.
- Alexander first offered Thebes a lenient settlement, demanding only the two ringleaders of the revolt and a general pardon for everyone else; the Thebans refused and counter-demanded two of his own officers, so he destroyed the city, killing roughly six thousand and selling some thirty thousand survivors into slavery, sparing only priests, known Macedonian sympathizers, and the poet Pindar's family.
- Amid the sack, a Theban matron named Timoclea, after being assaulted by a Thracian captain hunting for hidden treasure, lured him to a well under pretense of showing him her valuables and pushed him in, killing him with stones; brought before Alexander and asked who she was, she identified herself as the sister of Theagenes, who died fighting Philip at Chaeronea, and Alexander freed her and her children.
- Alexander then reversed his severity toward Athens, forgiving the city entirely despite its support for Thebes, and Plutarch notes Alexander later regretted the destruction of Thebes and blamed misfortunes like Clitus's murder on the wrath of Bacchus, patron god of Thebes.
- At the Isthmus of Corinth the assembled Greek states named Alexander general for the coming war against Persia; there the philosopher Diogenes, sunning himself and unimpressed by the visiting king, answered Alexander's offer of any favor by asking him only to "stand from between me and the sun," prompting Alexander to remark that if he were not Alexander, he would wish to be Diogenes.
- At Delphi, arriving on a day when the oracle was forbidden to speak, Alexander physically pressed the priestess toward the temple until, exasperated, she blurted "thou art invincible," a Delphic pronouncement he immediately declared sufficient and needing no further consultation.

### Crossing to Asia and the Battle of Granicus ()
Cite as: [Source: "Crossing to Asia and the Battle of Granicus"]
Principle: Alexander invades a continent by giving away nearly everything he owns and keeping only his hopes, then proves at Granicus that his own body will be the first thing risked in every battle that follows.
